title: Vision Zero plan and advisory committee redesign approved
subtitle: Sensitive public spaces near schools, property tax policy, governance review, single-use items by-law and AMO board support.
overview: Council approved the Vision Zero Action Plan for Safe Streets with two amendments, along with a Community Safety Zone Policy that takes effect July 1, 2025 {{vote:m13}}. One amendment requires council approval before general traffic lanes are converted to dedicated transit lanes {{vote:m11}}. Staff will also bring back a revised Traffic By-law in preparation for future automated enforcement.

Council approved new terms of reference for a redesigned set of advisory committees, replacing many existing bodies, and broadened the expertise sought for the Heritage committee {{vote:m9}}. On public space, council added spaces that share a property line with a school or childcare centre to the by-law's definition of sensitive public space {{vote:m17}}, after rejecting a referral to the Accessibility Advisory Committee {{vote:m16}}.

Council also passed, on consent, the 2025 property tax ratios and rates, governance review changes and a single-use items by-law, and supported the mayor's appointment to the Association of Municipalities of Ontario board. Before the open meeting, a closed session on the Enbridge municipal franchise agreement ended with council receiving information and giving direction to staff.

decisions.detail: Council approved the Vision Zero Guelph Action Plan for Safe Streets as amended, a Community Safety Zone Policy effective July 1, 2025, and a staff report-back with a revised Traffic By-law ahead of automated enforcement.
Action 4 of the plan was amended so converting general traffic lanes to dedicated transit lanes needs City Council approval before implementation.
Council approved terms of reference and policies for the new advisory committees and set the dissolution of a number of existing committees once the new ones are appointed and have met.
The Public Space Use By-law now defines public spaces sharing a property line with a school or childcare centre as sensitive public spaces {{vote:m17}}.
Council approved the 2025 property tax ratios and corresponding tax rates as part of the consent report.
Council approved a new Procedure By-law, a Pregnancy and Parental Leave Policy, a broader definition of newspaper in the public notice policy, and Delegation of Authority By-law amendments.
Council approved the additional phase 2 recommendation on reusable containers and the amended Single-Use Items By-law.
Council supported Mayor Cam Guthrie's appointment as Director, Large Urban Caucus, on the Association of Municipalities of Ontario Board for the 2024-2026 term.

debate: A delegate on Vision Zero urged that transit not be weakened while safety work proceeds, arguing the current network does not work for most residents and that better transit would reduce car dependence.

On requiring council approval for transit lane conversions, supporters said big changes should be decided publicly so councillors are accountable rather than pointing to an approved policy. Staff said the Quality Transit Network was already approved in 2022 but had no concern about returning to council.

On speed cameras, councillors asked about visibility and the delay before tickets arrive. Staff said extra signs are posted beyond provincial requirements and that a vendor is piloting faster image delivery. One councillor stressed the cameras should not be seen as a revenue source.

On the referral to the Accessibility Advisory Committee, supporters cited possible legal challenges, effects on people with disabilities within the unhoused population, and the short time school boards had to respond. Opponents said the item had been public for two weeks, the by-law had already been reviewed by that committee, and the change only clarifies a definition.

On the sensitive space definition, supporters cited clarity and protecting children, noting staff reported no school complaints so far. Opponents said it was overly broad, would push people away from services, and risked linking encampments with danger. A delegate also raised concerns about criminalizing people who cannot access shelters.
